title: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE… BUT THEN HE EXPOSED THE HEARTBREAKING REASON GOD NEVER WANTED IT THIS WAY
paragraphs: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE… BUT THEN HE EXPOSED THE HEARTBREAKING REASON GOD NEVER WANTED IT THIS WAY

One sentence from Jesus in Matthew 19:8 reveals something most people miss about marriage, divorce, hardened hearts, and the difference between what God permits in a broken world and what He intended from the beginning. And if you've ever loved someone who broke your heart, stayed in a marriage that was falling apart, or carried the shame of divorce, you need to hear what Jesus actually said.
There is something terrifying about a heart that can watch someone cry… and no longer feel anything.
Someone who once promised, “I will never leave you,” can eventually look into the eyes of the person they married and say, “I don't love you anymore.”
The same hands that once held each other in prayer now point fingers.
The same home that once echoed with laughter becomes a place where two people barely speak.
And sometimes the most heartbreaking moment isn't when someone walks out the door.
It's when you realize their heart left long before their body did.
But here is the question that should make every Christian stop and examine the Scriptures:
If God created marriage to be a lifelong covenant, why did Moses permit divorce?
Was God changing His mind?
Was divorce suddenly acceptable?
Or was something far more devastating happening inside the human heart?
Jesus answered that question nearly two thousand years ago.
And His answer was not what the religious leaders expected.
In Matthew 19, the Pharisees approached Jesus with a question that sounded theological but carried a trap beneath it.
“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?” (Matthew 19:3, KJV)
Notice what they were asking.
Not whether a marriage could be healed.
Not how a wounded husband and wife might find restoration.
Not how to protect a spouse who had been abandoned or mistreated.
They wanted to know how easily a man could end his marriage.
And that question exposed something about the culture surrounding them.
Marriage had become a subject of legal argument, and divorce could be discussed in terms of permissible grounds rather than the sacred responsibility of covenant love.

Among Jewish interpreters of the period, there were different understandings of the divorce provision in Deuteronomy 24:1. Some interpreted its grounds more narrowly, particularly in connection with sexual misconduct, while others allowed a broader range of reasons.
The Pharisees were drawing Jesus into that controversy.
But Jesus refused to begin where they wanted Him to begin.
They wanted to talk about the exit.
Jesus took them back to the entrance.
They wanted to discuss how a marriage could be dissolved.
Jesus reminded them why marriage existed.
He said:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?”
— Matthew 19:4–5, KJV
Then He declared:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
— Matthew 19:6, KJV
Read that again.
What God has joined together, let no human being tear apart.
Jesus was not presenting marriage as a disposable arrangement.

He was taking His listeners back to Genesis, before sin entered the world, before betrayal fractured relationships, before selfishness poisoned love, and before human hearts learned to justify what they were never created to desire.
He was showing them the Father's original design.
And then came the question.
“Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away?”
— Matthew 19:7, KJV
There it is.
The apparent contradiction.
If marriage was intended to be permanent, why did Moses give instructions concerning divorce?
And this is where Jesus spoke words that should shake anyone who has ever used a biblical permission as an excuse to avoid biblical responsibility.
“He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
— Matthew 19:8, KJV
Because of the hardness of your hearts.
Not because God's original design had failed.
Not because covenant faithfulness had become unimportant.
Not because love was supposed to disappear whenever circumstances became difficult.
Because human hearts had become hard.
And those words become even more powerful when we look at the language in which Matthew's Gospel was written.
The Greek text of Matthew 19:8 begins:
Πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
Pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn.
Meaning, in context, “Because of your hardness of heart.”
The word σκληροκαρδία (sklērokardia) combines the ideas of hardness and heart.
It describes a stubborn, resistant condition of the inner person.
A heart that resists what God desires.
A heart unwilling to yield.
A heart that can become so fixed in its own way that it refuses correction.
And suddenly this passage is no longer only about ancient divorce regulations.
It is about the frightening things that happen when the human heart stops listening to God.
A husband can become so consumed with pride that he refuses to apologize.
A wife can become so wounded that bitterness begins to replace every possibility of honest conversation.
A couple can spend years defending themselves while refusing to examine the ways they have harmed each other.
Someone can use religious language to disguise selfishness.
Someone can quote Scripture while refusing to practice mercy.
And sometimes a person can demand loyalty from a spouse while repeatedly violating the very covenant they claim to defend.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus was not declaring that every divorced person is hard-hearted.
He was explaining why divorce had been permitted within Israel's fallen social reality.
The one seeking divorce may be the one hardening their heart. The one being abandoned may have pleaded for reconciliation for years.
An innocent spouse can suffer the consequences of another person's unfaithfulness, cruelty, or refusal to repent.
The existence of a divorce does not, by itself, tell us who sinned, who suffered, or who tried to save the marriage.
And if we miss that distinction, we can turn the words of Jesus into a weapon against the very people who need His compassion.
Think about the woman who spent years praying for her marriage while her husband continued an affair.
Think about the man who desperately wanted to keep his family together while his wife repeatedly abandoned their commitments.
Think about the spouse who had to flee violence to protect themselves and their children.
Think about the person sitting quietly in church, wondering whether God still sees them as worthy of love because their marriage ended.
Jesus was not giving religious people permission to crush wounded souls.
He was confronting the human tendency to treat covenant commitments casually.
And to understand His answer, we must return to the passage the Pharisees were using.

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 describes a situation in which a man divorces his wife, gives her a written certificate, and sends her away. The passage then addresses what happens if she marries another man and that second marriage also ends.
The Hebrew expression associated with the written certificate is:
סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת
Sefer keritut.
Literally, a “document of cutting off,” commonly understood as a certificate of divorce.
The word keritut carries the idea of severance.
A marriage relationship that had joined two people was being legally dissolved.
But here is the detail that changes how we understand the Pharisees' argument.
Deuteronomy 24 did not command husbands to divorce their wives.
Its legal instruction addressed a particular situation involving divorce and remarriage, especially prohibiting the first husband from taking the woman back after her intervening marriage had ended.
The passage regulated a broken social reality.
It did not establish divorce as God's ideal.
The Pharisees spoke as though Moses had commanded divorce.
Jesus corrected their framing.
In Matthew 19:8, the Greek verb translated “suffered” in the King James Version is ἐπέτρεψεν (epetrepsen), meaning “permitted” or “allowed.”
There is a world of difference between a command and a permission.
God's moral ideal is not automatically identical to everything His law regulates in a fallen world.
Consider that for a moment.
A law may address the consequences of wrongdoing without celebrating the wrongdoing itself.
A legal provision may restrain harm without describing the perfect condition God originally intended.
That is the distinction Jesus was making.
Moses permitted divorce because of human hardness of heart.
But Jesus immediately added:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Those words matter.
Because Jesus did not measure marriage by the lowest standard people could legally defend.
He measured it by the Creator's intention.
And there is something deeply convicting about that.
We often ask, “How much can I do and still be right with God?”
Jesus calls us to ask, “What kind of heart reflects the character of my Father?”
We ask how far we can go before something becomes sin.
Jesus asks whether our hearts are being transformed by grace.
We ask what we can justify.
Jesus calls us to love what is good.
That is why this passage cannot be reduced to an argument about divorce certificates.
It is also a revelation of what sin does to the human heart.
In Genesis 2:24, Scripture says that a man shall leave his father and mother, cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
Basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying the same address.
Not simply a romantic partnership that continues only while feelings remain strong.
Marriage is presented as a profound union in which two lives are joined in a covenantal relationship.
The Hebrew verb used for “cleave” in Genesis 2:24 is דָּבַק (davaq), conveying the idea of clinging, holding fast, or remaining closely attached.
Marriage, in God's design, was never supposed to be treated like something people discard when it becomes inconvenient.
But this does not mean that staying physically present while practicing violence, coercion, humiliation, or persistent betrayal fulfills God's vision for marriage.
A marriage covenant is not honored merely because two people remain under the same roof.
Covenant faithfulness involves truth, love, responsibility, and care.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
That is sacrificial love.
Not domination.
Not intimidation.
Not using Scripture to demand obedience while refusing accountability.
And Ephesians 5:21 calls believers to mutual submission in reverence for Christ.
The pattern of Christian marriage cannot be separated from the character of Jesus.
The same Jesus who defended marriage also exposed religious hypocrisy.
The same Jesus who called people to repentance also showed compassion to the wounded.
The same Jesus who upheld God's commands refused to make human suffering invisible.
And this brings us to a question many readers may be afraid to ask.
Does Jesus mean that divorce is never permitted under any circumstances?
We must allow the Scriptures to speak carefully.
Immediately after explaining the hardness of heart, Jesus said:
“And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.”
— Matthew 19:9, KJV
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία (porneia), a term referring broadly to sexual immorality.
Christians differ over the precise scope of this exception and its implications for remarriage, but the exception itself must not be ignored.
Jesus was not teaching that sexual betrayal is insignificant.
He was condemning the casual dismissal of marriage while explicitly addressing sexual immorality as a serious matter.
The apostle Paul also addressed abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7:15:
“But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.”
Christians have long debated how this passage applies to divorce and remarriage. Some traditions understand abandonment as grounds for divorce, while others interpret the implications more narrowly.
And the Bible does not give a single, universally agreed-upon divorce formula covering every modern situation, particularly abuse.
Nevertheless, no faithful reading of Scripture should use marriage vows to require someone to remain exposed to violence or danger.
Seeking safety, involving appropriate authorities, protecting children, and establishing necessary separation can be morally responsible actions.
Reconciliation, where it is possible, requires more than tears, promises, or religious appearances.
It requires truth.
It requires repentance.
It requires changed behavior.
It requires accountability.
And where abuse has occurred, genuine repentance must never be used to pressure someone into immediate trust or unsafe reunion.
Forgiveness is a Christian calling. Reconciliation is not something one person can accomplish alone.
That distinction could save someone from years of unnecessary suffering.
Because some people have been taught that forgiveness means pretending nothing happened.
That grace means removing every boundary.
That being a good Christian means accepting repeated harm without protest.
But biblical forgiveness does not turn evil into good.
And Christian love does not require calling cruelty holy.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance precisely because sin matters.
Now imagine standing among the crowd that day, listening to Jesus.
The Pharisees have brought their legal question.
Jesus has taken them back to creation.
And suddenly the discussion is no longer comfortable.
Because it is easier to debate divorce than to confront selfishness.
It is easier to quote Moses than to admit you have stopped loving sacrificially.
It is easier to find a loophole than to confess you have been treating another human being as disposable.
And perhaps that is where this passage finds some of us today.
Not in a courtroom.
Not in a theological debate.
But sitting at the edge of a bed after another argument.
Looking at an unanswered message.
Wondering when affection turned into resentment.
Remembering a wedding day that now feels like another lifetime.
Or staring at a divorce certificate while trying to understand how something once filled with hope became a source of grief.
Maybe you are the one who walked away.
Maybe you were the one left behind.
Maybe you made choices you deeply regret.
Maybe you were faithful, but the other person was not.
Maybe you are still married, but something in your relationship has been dying quietly for years.
And perhaps the question you carry is not merely, “What does Matthew 19 mean?”
Perhaps your real question is:
“What does Jesus think of someone like me?”
That is where we must be especially careful not to stop reading the Bible too soon.
Because Matthew 19 reveals the seriousness of God's design for marriage.
But the Gospel also reveals the depth of God's mercy toward sinners.
In John 4, Jesus encountered a Samaritan woman whose relationship history was complicated.
He told her that she had had five husbands and that the man she was then with was not her husband.
We are not told all the circumstances behind those relationships.
Scripture does not authorize us to invent her motives, assume every marriage ended because of her wrongdoing, or treat her as nothing more than a moral failure.
What we do know is that Jesus knew the truth about her life.
And He still spoke to her.
He still offered her living water.
He still revealed profound spiritual truth to her.
And she went into her community speaking about the man who had told her what she had done.
That encounter reminds us of something beautiful.
Jesus does not need to deny the truth about your past in order to offer you a future.
He knows.
He sees.
He understands more than the people who have judged you.
And His grace is not limited by the chapters of your life that you wish you could rewrite.
But grace is not permission to keep destroying what God calls holy.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that misunderstanding directly.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes a new life possible.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to teach better relationship rules.
He came to rescue sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who turn to Him in faith.
That is why the words “from the beginning it was not so” carry such weight.
They remind us that the brokenness we have normalized is not the final measure of God's goodness.
But the Gospel gives us something even greater than a return to the Garden.
It gives us a Savior who entered our fallen world to redeem people who could not repair themselves.
And here is the astonishing part.
When Scripture describes Christ's relationship with His people, it uses the language of covenant love.
Ephesians 5:31–32 connects the one-flesh mystery of marriage with Christ and the church.
Human marriage is not identical to Christ's saving relationship with His people, but it is meant to reflect something of His faithful, self-giving love.
That means Christian marriage should never be understood merely as two people trying to keep each other happy.
At its best, it becomes a living testimony to the patience, faithfulness, forgiveness, and sacrificial love of Jesus.
Yet even the healthiest human marriage remains imperfect.
And even those who have experienced divorce, widowhood, abandonment, or lifelong singleness are not spiritually incomplete.
Our ultimate hope is not found in being married.
Our ultimate hope is found in belonging to Christ.
A wedding ring cannot save your soul.
A divorce decree cannot place a repentant believer beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Your marital status is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And perhaps someone needs to hear that without another day of shame.
If you sinned against your spouse, stop hiding behind explanations that make your actions sound smaller than they were.
Confess the truth.
Repent.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept accountability.
Do not demand immediate forgiveness as though repentance gives you control over another person's healing.
If you have been betrayed, do not mistake someone else's sin for proof that you were unworthy of love.
If your marriage is struggling but both of you are willing and it is safe to do so, seek wise, biblically grounded counsel and take honest steps toward healing.
If you are in danger, seek safety and trustworthy help.
If you are divorced, do not allow the loudest voices around you to become louder than the Gospel.
Study the Scriptures.
Seek wise pastoral guidance that takes your actual circumstances seriously.
And remember that Jesus calls every one of us to truth, repentance, faith, and obedience—not to endless self-condemnation.
There is another passage that makes the warning about hard hearts even more personal.
In Ezekiel 36:26, God promised:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.”
The Hebrew speaks of a לֵב הָאֶבֶן (lev ha'even), a heart of stone, and a לֵב בָּשָׂר (lev basar), a heart of flesh.
A stone heart is unresponsive.
A heart of flesh is living and responsive.
In its original context, this promise concerns God's restoration of His people and His work of renewing them through His Spirit.
It is not a guarantee that every broken marriage will be restored.
But it reveals the transforming character of God's grace.
The Lord does not merely tell His people to behave differently.
He promises to work within them.
To replace stubborn resistance with a heart responsive to Him.
To make obedience possible through His Spirit.
And that is the kind of transformation every relationship desperately needs.
Not merely better arguments.
Not merely more convincing apologies.
Not merely a temporary improvement after someone threatens to leave.
But hearts that are learning to surrender to God.
Hearts that tell the truth.
Hearts that refuse to use people.
Hearts that seek justice and practice mercy.
Hearts that understand love is more than emotion.
Because the tragedy of hardness of heart is not always that someone stops feeling love.
Sometimes it is that someone stops caring whether their actions are destroying another person.
And when Jesus spoke about divorce, He refused to let His listeners treat that destruction as a trivial legal matter.
He brought them back to the beginning.
Back to covenant.
Back to the Creator.
Back to the sacred value of the person standing beside them.
But He also stood among people who needed redemption.
People whose histories were already broken.
People whose choices had already caused suffering.
People who could not go backward and undo what had happened.
And that is why we must never preach Matthew 19 without remembering the cross.
The cross does not erase the seriousness of sin.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
And at the same time, it reveals a mercy greater than anything we could deserve.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is comfort for the abandoned.
There is strength for those rebuilding after devastation.
There is hope for those who have discovered that their own hearts have become hard.
Not because the past suddenly becomes harmless.
Not because every relationship will be restored.
Not because every consequence disappears.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem human lives even when their stories contain chapters they never wanted written.
That is what we mean when we say:
He does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
He rewrites our story by giving sinners forgiveness, a new identity, and a new direction through His death and resurrection.
He does not call darkness light.
He brings light into darkness.
He does not promise that every broken marriage will return to what it once was.
He promises that those who come to Him in faith will not be cast away (John 6:37).
And maybe that is the truth your heart has been waiting to hear.
You may not be able to change the day someone left.
You may not be able to recover the years that were lost.
You may not be able to undo the words that shattered trust.
You may not be able to restore a relationship that another person refuses to repair.
But you can bring your heart to Jesus today.
Not the polished version.
Not the religious version.
Not the version that pretends everything is fine.
The real one.
The exhausted one.
The grieving one.
The guilty one.
The angry one.
The one that still believes in God but is struggling to understand why life turned out this way.
And you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know where I have sinned, where I have been wounded, and where my heart has grown hard. Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your truth. Heal what is broken within me. Give me wisdom to obey You, courage to face what is true, and grace to forgive without pretending evil is good. Teach me to love as You command. Protect those who are vulnerable. Lead me in repentance, righteousness, and peace. Whatever happens with the relationships I cannot control, keep my heart close to You. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if this message has touched a place in your life that you rarely speak about, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to explain private circumstances publicly. You do not need to expose another person's sins. And you do not need to tell strangers details that could put you at risk.
But perhaps your prayer will remind another hurting person that they are not alone.
Perhaps someone reading the comments will discover that repentance is possible, that healing takes time, and that Christ has not abandoned them.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to condemn the divorced.
Not to pressure someone into returning to an unsafe relationship.
But to help people hear the words of Jesus in their biblical context, with both truth and compassion.
Our mission is not to build an audience around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
To the Scriptures.
To repentance.
To grace.
To forgiveness.
To redemption.
To a life transformed by the Gospel.
And certainly not because financial support can purchase God's favor.
Salvation is the gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something earned through payments, offerings, or religious activity (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And it teaches that such giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).

It is not a replacement for your responsibility to support your local church or care for your family. Rather, it is an additional opportunity to help make Gospel-centered resources available to more people.
Someone whose faith is growing cold.
Someone who is struggling through a broken marriage.
Someone who believes their past has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who may encounter a passage of Scripture at precisely the moment they need to hear the truth about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to participate in sharing the message of Jesus Christ.
A Facebook share helps introduce the message to new readers.
A thoughtful comment helps begin a conversation.
A saved article may become a Scripture study someone returns to in a difficult season.
A personal invitation may lead someone to explore the Gospel for the first time.
It is to place the truth of Scripture before human hearts, trusting the Holy Spirit to do what no writer, preacher, or ministry can accomplish by human strength.
To awaken conviction.
To point sinners toward repentance.
To remind the wounded of Christ's compassion.
To help believers grow in biblical understanding.
And to keep proclaiming that Jesus Christ is the only Savior who can reconcile us to God.
Now return with me, one last time, to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did Moses permit divorce when Jesus said, “From the beginning it was not so”?
Because God was dealing with human beings whose hearts had been corrupted by sin.
Moses' law regulated the consequences of that brokenness.
Jesus restored the conversation to God's original design.
And the Gospel reveals the Savior who can transform the hearts of those who turn to Him.
That is the answer.
Not a contradiction between Moses and Jesus.
Not evidence that God's holiness had changed.
Not permission to trivialize marriage.
And not a sentence of hopelessness over every person whose marriage has ended.
It is a revelation of the difference between the broken world human sin has produced and the good purpose of the God who created us.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one question.
Not merely whether you have ever been divorced.
Not merely whether your marriage is strong.
Not merely whether someone else has failed you.
Ask yourself:
“Lord, where has my heart become hard toward Your truth?”
Because the most dangerous heart is not always the one that has suffered heartbreak.
Sometimes it is the one that can no longer recognize its need to repent.
And the most beautiful evidence of grace is not a life with no scars.
It is a life that has surrendered its scars, its sins, its pride, and its future to Jesus Christ.
The Pharisees came asking how a marriage could end.
Jesus answered by reminding them why God created it.
And the cross reminds us that even when human beings have made a terrible mess of what God called good, His mercy still calls us to repentance and new life.
You cannot go back and rewrite the day your heart was broken—but you can surrender your heart to the Savior who was pierced to bring broken sinners home.
